source_acquisition.search_note: The proceedings PDF is the Figure/Table inventory fact source: it has 36 pages, 19 figures, 19 tables, and Algorithms 1–5. The reading record and reports/tables/visual_source_inventory.csv select tile-ai/tilelang with exact_visual_source and an explicit PDF URL. The local corpus/visual_sources directory contains the 11 acquired files listed above. GitHub main was checked at commit 8ef052f1515d463603b76741d6760d76ec0c5917 using gh repository view and recursive tree/API; the repository exposes layout plotting code and several SVG assets but no paper-specific Figure 1–19 TeX or benchmark-plot generator. Therefore source provenance is exact for the linked TileLang visual tooling and PDF objects, while object-level styling observations rely on the rendered conference PDF. All 36 PDF pages were rendered at 200 dpi (1700 x 2200 px) and inspected, including body, references, and appendix.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Plots use local pastel categorical palettes for method/library identity, with direct labels and marker or hatch redundancy where available. Method/benchmark charts use blue, orange, green, purple, gold, gray, red, and brown accents; diagrams use pastel fills for stages, layouts, and hardware roles; code figures use syntax highlighting; tables are grayscale black text with booktabs or partial-grid rules. Color is not a single paper-wide quantitative scale.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: The conference PDF is predominantly vector text, rules, arrows, diagrams, code, and table geometry. Figures 1, 4, 8, 9, and 10 contain rasterized or mixed chart components; Figures 2, 12–19 are code screenshots/listings with mixed text and highlight objects; diagrams in Figures 3, 5–7, and 11 combine vector geometry with embedded raster-like panels. At 200 dpi all objects remain present, but several labels are below comfortable reading size.
paper_style.style_consistency: The two-column ICLR layout, Roman body/caption typography, monospace code, grayscale tables, and compact booktabs/partial-grid rules are consistent. Figures 1, 8, and 10 share a LOC-versus-speedup grammar, while the method diagrams share arrow-and-box vocabulary. Palette semantics, caption completeness, uncertainty definitions, and exact cross-links are less consistent across objects.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Performance vs. code size trade-off for MLA kernels on NVIDIA H100. Points closer to the top-left indicate better balance between performance and implementation simplicity. The annotated speedup values indicate performance gains over the PyTorch implementation.

color.semantic_mapping: Method or library identity is encoded by color; point text and position carry the primary comparison.

encodings.text: direct speedup labels and whisker-like vertical ranges

figures.data_and_statistics: Four implementation points compare LOC with relative MLA speedup on H100. The y-axis is logarithmic; the visible vertical ranges are rendered as uncertainty/error-like marks, but the caption does not define whether they are repeated-run variability or another range.
figures.evidence_relation: Opening problem framing → the top-left design target → Figure 8's cross-operator H100/MI300X comparison and Figure 10's GEMM comparison. It motivates the method without replacing the later benchmark tables.
design_strengths: Two axes expose the claimed performance-versus-programmability trade-off directly.
Top-left ideal direction and direct speedup labels reduce lookup cost.
A compact single-column inset fits beside the introductory prose.
design_weaknesses: Whisker semantics, run count, and aggregation are not defined in the caption.
The pastel colors are not paired with a shape or line key that remains robust in grayscale.
Very small point labels and a log axis make exact low-speedup values difficult to read at page scale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use an explicit Pareto scatter with a declared ideal direction, direct numeric labels, and redundant method encoding; define any whisker or range in the caption.

figures.evidence_relation: Section 3 interface example → Figure 3's two-stage workflow → Figures 5–7's layout, pipeline, and compiler mechanisms. It grounds abstract stages in concrete API usage.

Stage colors are not reused consistently enough across all later diagrams.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Tile recommendation with cost model. In (b), we show a scatter plot of candidate schedules. The x-axis orders candidates by their predicted latency, and the y-axis shows their normalized scores defined as latency of best candidate / latency of current candidate which lies in the range (0,1].

color.semantic_mapping: Pastel fills distinguish pipeline stages, operator roles, schedule states, and architecture blocks; arrows and labels carry redundant structure.

encodings.x: candidate rank or predicted latency in panel b
encodings.facet: a: hardware-aligned search; b: candidate scatter; c: interactive schedule

figures.data_and_statistics: Panel (a) sketches hardware-aligned candidate generation, panel (b) plots candidate schedules ordered by predicted latency against normalized score, and panel (c) shows an interactive schedule representation. The score is bounded in (0,1]; candidate marks are not accompanied by a sampling or uncertainty statement.
figures.evidence_relation: Cost-model description → Figure 4's recommendation mechanism → Table 3's predicted-top-5% retention → Figure 11's cooperative recommendation/inference workflow. It is the core method-to-evidence bridge.
design_strengths: Three panels move from mechanism to quantitative candidate ranking to user-facing schedule.
Panel labels and the explicit normalized-score formula make the intended reading order clear.
The wide placement gives the scatter and schedule enough room for labels.
design_weaknesses: Panel b's axes and candidate density are difficult to recover at PDF page scale.
The caption defines the score but not the cost-model inputs, candidate count, or any error semantics.
Pastel colors carry several local roles without a global legend or grayscale redundancy.
figures.reusable_pattern: Sequence a conceptual search diagram, a compact diagnostic scatter, and a concrete schedule view; define the normalized score beside the plot rather than in a detached paragraph.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: The visual narrative moves from the LOC/speedup motivation (Figures 1 and 10), through concrete code and compiler mechanisms (Figures 2–7), to cross-operator/hardware results and ablation (Figures 8–9), then to appendix architecture diagrams, source listings, and workload inventories (Figures 11–19 and Tables 1–19).
cross_object_system.caption_system: Captions use a consistent Figure/Table label and short title, but only Figures 1, 4, 8 and Table 3 define encodings or a headline finding in enough detail. Most code and mechanism captions identify the object without defining abbreviations, color roles, fixed workload parameters, or omitted content.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Tables use one header level, left-aligned textual fields, centered or right-aligned numeric fields, and black booktabs or partial-grid rules. Row-group structure appears in Table 1 and Table 8; shape inventories use stable configuration IDs but generally do not provide a second grouped header.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figures 5–7 and Algorithms 1–5 explain layout and pipeline inference, Figure 9 isolates Tile/Alloc/Partition contributions, and Figures 8/10 plus Tables 3–10 report broader performance/LOC consequences. The link is conceptually strong, but captions rarely point to exact implementation regions or shape rows.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: The appendix supplies Table 1/2 primitives and hardware specifications, Table 3 cost-model retention, Figures 11–14 architecture/code evidence, Figures 15–19 kernel listings, and Tables 4–19 benchmark/shapes/provenance. Main figures reference these ideas, but many appendix objects require the surrounding prose to define identifiers.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Roman figure captions and table text are stable, while code uses a small monospace face. Plot labels and diagram annotations vary in size and embedded font, producing a repeated page-scale readability issue in dense multi-panel objects.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Colors are locally coherent within individual plots or diagrams, and hatching appears in the ablation, but method colors and stage colors are not globally fixed across all figures. Grayscale safety is therefore partial; direct labels and geometry provide the main redundancy.

most_reusable_patterns: LOC-versus-speedup Pareto scatter with an explicit ideal direction, direct labels, and a declared method key.
Cumulative grouped ablation bars with a fixed baseline, architecture facets, and hatch redundancy.
Matched source/lowered IR or architecture code panes connected by stable region or operation identifiers.
Stable workload-shape inventories with IDs that can be cited by code examples and performance tables.
highest_value_objects: Figure 8: repeated H100/MI300X operator panels make the central performance/programmatic trade-off comparable across hardware and workloads.
Figure 9: staged ablation connects compiler mechanisms to architecture-specific gains.
Figure 4: the three-panel recommendation figure combines mechanism, candidate ranking, and schedule output.
Table 3: cost-model screening claim is stated with an operational top-5%/pruning interpretation.
failure_patterns: Unexplained vertical range or whisker marks recur in the quantitative scatter plots.
Dense multi-panel and code figures use labels near the minimum readable size and omit caption keys.
Appendix shape inventories and baseline tables rarely map stable IDs or commits directly to individual result objects.
Local pastel palettes are not a paper-wide semantic system and are only partly redundant in grayscale.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: TileLang combines repeated LOC-versus-speedup trade-off plots with compiler-stage schematics, architecture-specific ablations, and reproducibility-oriented code/shape inventories, but its evidence system would be stronger with globally stable encodings and explicit range, shape, and identifier definitions.
